title: Using kan, vil, må, and skal
goal: Build simple sentences with kan, vil, må, and skal plus a bare infinitive.

objectives.statement: Build simple sentences with kan, vil, må, and skal plus a bare infinitive.

spans.value: It is Saturday morning. Nora and Amir share a flat in Oslo. They are deciding what to do before Nora’s sister visits in the afternoon.
Hva skal du gjøre i dag?

blocks.translation: What are you going to do today?

spans.value: Ja, men jeg må gå nå. Butikken stenger tidlig.

blocks.translation: Yes, but I have to leave now. The shop closes early.

spans.value: Vent litt. Jeg vil lage suppe, så vi må kjøpe grønnsaker.

blocks.translation: Wait a moment. I want to make soup, so we have to buy vegetables.

spans.value: Greit. Skal vi spise hjemme i kveld?

blocks.translation: All right. Shall we eat at home this evening?

spans.value: Ja. Søsteren min kan komme klokka seks.

blocks.translation: Yes. My sister can come at six.

spans.value: Da skal jeg kjøpe litt ekstra mat.

blocks.translation: Then I’ll buy some extra food.

spans.value: The conversation contains four very useful verbs:
. Nora and Amir use them to talk about ability or possibility, wishes, necessity, and plans. Each one is followed by another verb:
Notice something important: the second verb does not have

sections.title: One sentence pattern, four meaning choices

spans.value: You already know that Norwegian often uses the infinitive marker
, however, the infinitive marker disappears. The second verb is a
The form of the modal verb does not change with the subject:
The main decision is therefore not which ending to use. It is which meaning you want: ability or possibility, desire, necessity, or a plan.
when someone is able to do something or when something is possible.

en.value: I can speak a little Norwegian.

spans.value: describes what a person is able to do.

no.value: Søsteren min kan komme klokka seks.

en.value: My sister can come at six.

spans.value: presents six o’clock as possible. Compare:

en.value: She is going to come today.

spans.value: The first sentence says that coming today is possible. The second presents it as her plan.
A common mistake is to add

sections.title: Vil: what someone wants to do

spans.value: before a bare infinitive to say what someone wants to do.

en.value: The children want to play outside.
We want to see the film.

spans.value: can have future uses too, but in the simple personal sentences in this lesson, read it primarily as

en.value: I want to buy a bicycle.

spans.value: she is expressing a wish. She is not necessarily reporting a settled plan.

no.value: Jeg skal besøke Bergen på fredag.

en.value: I am going to visit Bergen on Friday.

spans.value: The first sentence expresses desire. The second presents a plan.

en.value: We want to eat at home.
We want to eat at home.

spans.value: when something is necessary: someone must do it or has to do it.

en.value: You have to wait a little.
Sara has to work this evening.
I have to call the doctor.
We have to take the bus.

spans.value: The action is the same, but the reason is different.
comes from what the speaker wants.
A learner may be tempted to translate English “to” directly:

statement.value: is followed directly by the bare infinitive.

spans.value: with a bare infinitive to present an intended or arranged action. English often uses “am/is/are going to” in the translation.
At the beginning of the dialogue, Amir says:
He has a plan. Later he adjusts it:

no.value: Jeg skal kjøpe litt ekstra mat.
Jeg skal møte Eva klokka tre.

en.value: I’m going to meet Eva at three.

no.value: De skal reise til Trondheim i morgen.

en.value: They are going to travel to Trondheim tomorrow.

no.value: Vi skal spise hjemme i kveld.

en.value: We are going to eat at home this evening.
Mina is going to work on Saturday.

spans.value: Compare the four modal verbs with the same main verb:

en.value: I am going to make dinner.

spans.value: These sentences do not describe four different actions. They show four different ways of viewing the same action:

items.value: presents a plan or intended action.

no.value: ✗ De skal å reise i morgen.

en.value: They are going to travel tomorrow.
They are going to travel tomorrow.

spans.value: The shared grammar pattern is easy to see, but choosing the correct modal requires attention to the situation.
Imagine that Jonas is talking about a concert:

en.value: Jonas can go to the concert.
Jonas wants to go to the concert.
Jonas has to go to the concert.
Jonas is going to go to the concert.

spans.value: He is able to go, or going is possible.
stays the same. The modal verb changes the meaning.

en.value: We want to take the train.
We have to take the train.
We are going to take the train.

spans.value: When you build such sentences, make two decisions:

items.value: Which bare infinitive names the action?

spans.value: Amir is now ready to leave. Nora checks the plan one more time.
Ja, det kan jeg. Hva vil du spise til dessert?

blocks.translation: Yes, I can. What do you want to eat for dessert?

spans.value: Jeg vil lage eplekake, men jeg må kjøpe epler.

blocks.translation: I want to make apple cake, but I have to buy apples.

spans.value: Greit. Jeg skal kjøpe epler også.

blocks.translation: All right. I’ll buy apples too.

spans.value: Flott. Da kan vi spise eplekake i kveld.

blocks.translation: Great. Then we can eat apple cake this evening.

spans.value: The four choices now have clear jobs in the scene:

items.value: Nora asks about Amir’s ability with
Nora presents a future possibility with

spans.value: All five combinations use a bare infinitive.
The most important form mistake is placing
between the modal and the action verb.
Changing the modal for the subject
Do not add a special ending because the subject changes.
Choosing by action rather than meaning
No action verb automatically belongs with one modal.

en.value: I am going to eat now.

spans.value: Choose the modal from the intended meaning, not from the action itself.

sections.title: Transfer: preparing for a day trip

spans.value: Now change the situation. Lea and Henrik are preparing for a Sunday trip to the forest. They have a plan, but they also have practical needs and personal wishes.

Lea is able to drive. Henrik wants to take photographs. They have to leave before nine. They are going to meet their friend Mari at the station. Later, good weather may make an outdoor lunch possible.

Without looking back, recall the four modal verbs and complete one new sentence for each meaning: something you can do, something you want to do, something you have to do, and something you are going to do. Keep every sentence simple, and place the action verb directly after

prompt.value: Complete each short sentence with the bare infinitive that follows the modal. Choose the form without å.
Build the Norwegian sentence for this ability: You are able to cook.
Build the Norwegian sentence for this desire: Mina wants to eat at home.
Choose the option that matches both situations, in order: 1. Nora wants to go home. 2. Nora has to go home.

options.text: Nora vil gå hjem. Nora må gå hjem.
options.why: The first sentence uses vil for desire; the second uses må for necessity. Both use the bare infinitive gå.

options.text: Nora må gå hjem. Nora vil gå hjem.
options.why: The meanings are in the opposite order.

stem.value: Choose the Norwegian sentences that express the two meanings in the stated order.

prompt.value: Build the Norwegian sentence for this planned arrangement: You are going to eat at home this evening.

Choose the set of four Norwegian sentences that matches the situations in order: 1. Jonas is able to make dinner. 2. Jonas wants to make dinner. 3. Jonas has to make dinner. 4. Jonas is going to make dinner.

options.text: Jonas kan å lage middag. Jonas vil å lage middag. Jonas må å lage middag. Jonas skal å lage middag.
options.why: The infinitive marker å must not appear after these modal verbs.

options.text: Jonas vil lage middag. Jonas kan lage middag. Jonas skal lage middag. Jonas må lage middag.
options.why: The modal choices do not match the four meanings in order.

options.text: Jonas kan lage middag. Jonas vil lage middag. Jonas må lage middag. Jonas skal lage middag.
options.why: The modals match ability, desire, necessity, and plan in order, and each is followed directly by lage.

stem.value: Select the set with the correct modal for each meaning and a bare infinitive after every modal.

prompt.value: Build four Norwegian sentences in this order for Nora and Amir: Nora wants to make soup; Nora has to buy vegetables; Amir is going to buy some extra food; Nora can eat at home this evening.
Select the one extra token after the modal. The feedback explains the required bare-infinitive pattern.

payload.feedback: Remove å: after må, use the bare infinitive jobbe directly.

prompt.value: Build five Norwegian sentences in this order for the Sunday forest trip: Lea is able to drive; Henrik wants to take photographs; the group has to leave before nine; they are going to meet Mari at the station; if the weather is good later, an outdoor lunch is possible.

Build four new Norwegian sentences in this order: Lea can help you; Henrik wants to eat outside; Mina has to buy vegetables; Oskar is going to learn Norwegian. Use all four modal verbs once and place each modal directly before the bare infinitive.
